newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.AFRICAN MARCH PPI WEIGHED BY TECHNICALS.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.AFRICAN MARCH PPI WEIGHED BY TECHNICALS.

text.p: Technical factors and an upward trend in imported goods were seen the main drivers behind a 0.4 percentage point rise in the March year-on-year producer price inflation figure, according to analysts.
The data is scheduled for release next Thursday at 0900 GMT.
A Reuters consensus poll of eight economists forecast the overall producer price index would rise 0.1 percent month-on-month or 9.7 percent year-on-year after a 0.4 and 9.3 percent rise in February.
March consumer price inflation numbers only just beat market consensus at 0.6 percent month-on-month and 9.6 percent year-on-year.

"The main reason for the rise (in PPI) will be technical factors because it comes off a very low base of minus 0.2 percent in the corrresponding month-on-month figure last year," said SMK Securities economist Hermann van Papendorp.
In addition, pressure was seen from the imported manufacturing side.

"The actual upward pressure will probably still come from the imported side and that's mainly due to the rand's sharp depreciation last year...the lag periods are very long," Huysamer Stals economist Johann Roussouw noted.
He expected the imported trend to be up at 10.9 percent from 10.3 percent on a 0.1 percent month-on-month increase.
But this would be offset to some extent by a sharp decline in international crude oil prices over the last two months, economists agreed.
"In the last two months the rand/oil price fell by around 20 percent and this should keep the imported side lower," one said.

Imported inflation was the main contributor to the 0.4 percent month-on-month rise in the producer price index in February with the main increase in mining and quarrying product prices as well as chemicals and chemical product prices.
Economists were generally upbeat on the outlook for inflathon for the rest of the year with several predicting that the March 9.7 percent consensus could be the peak for the year.
"I would see the peak at 9.7 percent, not much higher. This is the top," said van Papendorp.
"It seems that the March figure (of 9.5 percent) might be the peak for the current cycle," Roussouw said.
"I'm very confident that both in the case of CPI and PPI we won't see double digits. In the case of CPI, it appears we have already peaked in February at 9.8 percent," he added.
Equisec's Roodt forecast the peak at around 9.6 percent and said the trend would probably be sideways for a month or two before inflation started dipping.
